title: Short links for university notices

authoring.author: Parikshaa content team
authoring.originality: Written for Parikshaa: our own short-link design case, examples, code, quiz and explanations; no text from any site, book or course.

scenario: The university sends exam notices by SMS, and SMS messages are short and charged per 160 characters. The IT cell wants a short-link service: `uni.in/x7Kq2` redirects to the long notice URL. Departments create links; students click them. Design it.

clarifying_questions.q: Who creates links, and how many?
clarifying_questions.a: About 200 staff accounts create around 2,000 links a day.
A notice sent to 1 lakh students gets most of its clicks in the first hour; about 20 lakh clicks a day overall.
Optionally, a creator sets an expiry; default is 2 years.
Allowed for staff (uni.in/results-2026), checked for clashes.
Yes, per link per day, but a few minutes of delay is fine.

functional: Create a short code for a long URL, optionally custom and with expiry
Redirect a short code to its URL
Count clicks per link per day

non_functional.name: Redirect latency
non_functional.target: p99 under 50 ms at the server

non_functional.name: Availability
non_functional.target: 99.9%; redirects matter more than link creation

estimates.question: Peak redirects per second if one notice to 1 lakh students gets 60% of its clicks in the first 10 minutes?
estimates.working: 1,00,000 × 0.6 = 60,000 clicks in 600 s = 100 per second for one notice; several notices at once multiply it.

estimates.question: How many distinct codes do 7 base-62 characters give, in billions (rounded)?
estimates.working: 62^7 ≈ 3.52 × 10^12 = about 3,522 billion: at 2,000 links a day that lasts far beyond any need.

estimates.question: Storage for 10 years of links at 500 bytes per link, in GB?

expected_components.name: Redirect service (stateless)
expected_components.why: Looks up a code and answers with an HTTP redirect; the hot path.

expected_components.name: Key-value store or relational table for code → URL
expected_components.why: Single-key lookups; a primary key index answers in one read.

expected_components.name: Cache in front of the store
expected_components.why: A few popular notices take most clicks, so caching hot codes removes most reads.

expected_components.name: Code generator
expected_components.why: Produces short, unique codes without clashes: a counter encoded in base 62, or random codes with a uniqueness check.

expected_components.name: Asynchronous click counting
expected_components.why: Writing a counter on every redirect would slow the hot path; log clicks to a queue and aggregate later.

expected_components.name: Admin API with authentication
expected_components.why: Only staff create or disable links.

expected_components.name: Abuse checks on target URLs
expected_components.why: Stops the short domain being used to disguise phishing links.

api: GET /{code} → 301/302 to the URL, 404 if unknown, 410 if disabled or expired
data_model: links(code PRIMARY KEY, url, created_by, created_at, expires_at, disabled); clicks_daily(code, day, count) built from a click log by a periodic job.

diagram.alt: Students' browsers hit the redirect service, which reads a cache and then the links table; each click is logged to a queue that an aggregator turns into daily counts; staff use an admin API that writes links with codes from a generator.

data.source:
flowchart LR
  B[Student browser] --> R[Redirect service]
  R --> C[(Hot code cache)]
  C --> L[(links table)]
  R -->|click event| Q[Queue]
  Q --> AG[Aggregator] --> D[(clicks_daily)]
  S[Staff] --> A[Admin API] --> G[Code generator]

deep_dives.body: Option 1: a database sequence gives 1, 2, 3 ... and we write the number in base 62 (digits, lower case, upper case). Codes are short and never clash, but they are guessable: anyone can try the next code and read unpublished notices. Option 2: random 7-character codes, inserted with the code as primary key; on the rare clash (about 73 lakh used out of 3.5 trillion) retry. Codes are unguessable. For notices that may be sent before they are public, **random codes are the safer choice**.

A 301 (permanent) redirect is cached by browsers, so repeat clicks never reach us: cheaper, but we lose those clicks in the counts and cannot disable a link the browser has cached. A 302 (temporary) brings every click to us. Because counts and the ability to disable a wrongly sent notice matter here, **use 302** and cache on our side instead.

trade_offs: Random codes cost a uniqueness check on creation but stop people guessing unpublished links.
302 redirects cost more traffic than 301 but keep counts accurate and links disable-able.
Counting clicks asynchronously makes stats a few minutes late but keeps redirects fast.
failure_modes: The links store is down: the cache still serves hot codes; new links cannot be created until it returns.
The click queue is down: redirects continue and click events are dropped or buffered locally; counts are slightly low.
A wrong notice was sent: disable the link and purge it from the cache, so new clicks get 410.

rubric.criterion: Clarifies read/write ratio, custom codes, expiry and counting needs.
Estimates peak redirects, code space and storage.
Chooses a code scheme and explains uniqueness and guessability.
Keeps the redirect path to a cache read and a redirect; counting off the hot path.
Covers disabling, expiry, abuse and failures.
Clear structure and trade-offs (AI feedback, advice only).

concept_checks.stem: Why might sequential base-62 codes be a problem for exam notices?
options: They are guessable, so unpublished notices can be found by trying the next code
concept_checks.explanation: Sequential codes reveal neighbours; random codes do not.

concept_checks.stem: Which redirect status keeps every click visible to the service?
concept_checks.explanation: Browsers cache 301s; 302s come back to the server each time.

concept_checks.stem: How many codes do 6 base-62 characters give, roughly?
Why count clicks through a queue instead of updating a counter in the redirect request?
options: It keeps the redirect fast and avoids contention on a hot counter row
concept_checks.explanation: A popular link's counter row would become a write hotspot on the critical path.

follow_ups: How would you show the target URL as a preview before redirecting, to build trust?
How would you shard the links table if it grew to billions of rows?
How would you detect a flood of clicks from bots?

revision_card.front: Short-link service: hot path, code scheme, redirect code?
revision_card.back: Hot path: cache → table lookup → 302 redirect; counting via a queue. Codes: random base-62 (unguessable) with a uniqueness retry, or sequence + base 62 (guessable). 302 keeps counts and disabling possible; 301 is cached by browsers.
